bib.title: Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators", William Saunders, Catherine Yeh, Jeff Wu (equal contribution), Steven Bills, Long Ouyang, Jonathan Ward, Jan Leike (OpenAI). Preprint, arXiv:2206.05802v2, 14 Jun 2022.

PDF: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/05-graph-engineering/sources/saunders-2022-self-critiquing-models-assisting-human.pdf

COVERAGE: I read 54 of 54 pages and all 165,161 characters were extracted. I read pp. 1–36 closely: the main text, limitations, Appendices A–E and the F intro. I also read the helpfulness samples (Tables 6–15) and two assistance samples (Tables 16–17). For pp. 41–54 (Tables 18–35, random assistance and refinement samples) I checked the captions and spot-read the text. They hold examples only and no results. I skimmed the references for origins.

Fit for graph engineering: this is a fine-tuning and scalable-oversight paper, not a multi-agent orchestration paper. Every role (answer, critique, critiqueability, helpfulness, refine) is played by one jointly trained model. It still gives clean evidence for a generator → critic → refiner loop and a critic-ranking (helpfulness-score) node.

CLAIMS
- claim: Model critiques shown to human evaluators raise the number of flaws they find by about 50%.
  number: ~50% more critiques
  setup: topic-based summarisation on held-out passages of 2048–3840 tokens. Labelers saw 8 model critiques (one each at temperatures 0.0–0.6 and 1.0), de-duplicated and sorted by helpfulness score. Critiques came from the best fine-tuned model. Answers were model-written, human-written or human-misleading.
  quote: "Human labelers asked to ﬁnd critiques of (model or human-written) answers ﬁnd about 50% more critiques when given assistance from a critique model."
  where: p.2, §1.2
- claim: On planted flaws (misleading answers written on purpose), assisted labelers found the intended flaw 45% of the time against 27% unassisted.
  number: 45±5% vs 27±5%
  setup: human-misleading answers whose authors wrote down the intended critique. The authors then judged whether other labelers found it.
  quote: "With assistance, labelers ﬁnd the intended critiques 45± 5% of the time, whereas without assistance they only ﬁnd it 27± 5% of the time."
  where: p.8, §3.3.1
- claim: Assistance does not lower the share of critiques the answer's author judges valid. It does raise the number of valid critiques.
  number: 71% vs 73% valid; 0.96±0.09 vs 0.62±0.07 valid critiques
  setup: same misleading-answer subset
  quote: "The fraction of critiques the author considers valid does not appreciably decrease with assistance (71% with assistance versus 73% without). 3. However, the number of valid critiques is still much higher, 0.96± 0.09 vs. 0.62± 0.07."
  where: p.8
- claim: Assisted labelers also found more valid critiques that were novel.
  number: 0.24±0.06 vs 0.18±0.05
  setup: same subset
  quote: "With assistance, labelers also ﬁnd more valid and novel critiques,0.24±0.06 vs. 0.18±0.05."
  where: p.8
- claim: With assistance, more model answers get flagged and they are rated lower.
  number: 54%→78% of inputs critiqued; rating 5.6→4.9
  setup: model answers, 1–7 Likert scale
  quote: "on model answers, unassisted labelers found critiques on just 54% of inputs and gave an average rating of 5.6, while assisted labelers found critiques on 78% of inputs and gave an average rating of 4.9."
  where: p.8
- claim: Labelers mostly accepted model critiques without editing them. This is a rubber-stamping risk for any human-in-the-loop critic.
  number: 15.3%
  setup: assist condition
  quote: "Only 15.3% of the used critiques were edited further."
  where: p.8
- claim: Assistance barely changes time spent. Showing 8 critiques beats showing 4.
  number: 6.27 / 5.82 / 6.26 min; 0.74 / 1.06 / 1.31 critiques
  setup: an earlier ablation run during the project
  quote: "No assistance 6.27± 0.31 0.74± 0.05 / 4 critiques 5.82± 0.27 1.06± 0.07 / 8 critiques 6.26± 0.27 1.31± 0.08"
  where: p.35-36, App. E.3
- claim: Larger models critique their own outputs better, even though their outputs are harder to critique.
  number: critiqueable outputs about 20% less often for the most capable models
  setup: 5 pretrained models, with scale measured as fine-tuning loss (nats/token), not parameter count. Self-critique was sampled at the same random temperature as the answer.
  quote: "More capable models have critiqueable outputs around 20% less often than the smallest models, ac-cording to labelers. Less than 15% of outputs are uncri-tiqueable for the worst models, and over 30% for the best models."
  where: p.10, Fig. 4a caption
- claim: Refining with a critique helps only for large models, and only beats direct refinement when the critique is chosen by best-of-N on the helpfulness score. Rejection sampling over direct refinements may be the stronger baseline at equal compute.
  number: none
  setup: win rate against the original best-of-1 answer, T=0.5, everything generated by one model
  quote: "Conditional reﬁnement appear to outperform direct reﬁnements, but only with critiques selected via best-of-N against helpfulness." / "Both forms of reﬁnement signiﬁcantly outperform the original output for larger models, but have little to no effect for smaller models." / "rejection sampling on direct reﬁnements appears to be a stronger baseline."
  where: p.12, §4.3.1
- claim: The GDC gap. A model can discriminate (tell an answer is flawed) better than it can critique (articulate the flaw), and on summarisation this critique-discrimination (CD) gap does not shrink with scale.
  number: none (shown in figures only)
  setup: best-of-2 against a discriminator (D) or a human-judged critique severity (C), compared with an average sample (G). Applied to summarisation and 4 synthetic tasks (Addition, 3-SAT, Alphabetize, RACE).
  quote: "We observe a positive CD gap for topic-based summarization and 3-SAT and negative gap for Addition and RACE. 3. For topic-based summarization, the CD gap is approximately constant across model scale."
  where: p.17, §5.3
- claim: Their critique model beats InstructGPT zero-shot and few-shot baselines but is still well below humans.
  number: none
  setup: helpfulness judged by humans on critiqueable answers
  quote: "Overall we ﬁnd our model’s critiques to be helpful more often than the baselines, but still substantially less helpful than human critiques (Figure 3)."
  where: p.9
- claim: Naive 2-step debate, which scores an answer by the helpfulness of its best-of-N critiques with no human involved, never matches a direct critiqueability discriminator at telling honest from misleading answers.
  number: none
  setup: largest model, T=0.5, paired honest and misleading answers
  quote: "The best-of-N helpfulness score appears to be asymptoting with N→∞ to worse than the critiqueability score. This suggests naive 2-step debate wouldn’t work as well as RLHP for this task."
  where: p.34, App. D
- claim: Humans reading a slate of 8 critiques judge answers better than humans reading 1 best-of-8 critique, and both beat a single critique. All three still fall short of the discriminator.
  number: none
  quote: "humans evaluating 8 critiques outperforms humans evaluating 1 optimized critique (Ch8 > C8). However, it still seems to fall short of discriminator ability."
  where: p.32
- claim: Labeler agreement on ranking critiques was about the same as on ranking answers.
  number: ~75%
  quote: "Agreement rate on comparisons of critiques (i.e. helpfulness rankings) were no higher than answer comparisons; both were around 75%."
  where: p.18
- claim: Training data is over 6,000 topical queries on over 2,000 passages. Helpfulness labels number 41,724 for training. Training was SFT only, one epoch.
  number: 6,000 / 2,000 / 41,724
  quote: "We collected our own dataset of over 6,000 distinct topical queries and summaries, on over 2,000 distinct passages."
  where: p.4; Table 4 p.25

LIMITS
- The authors concede (§7.2, p.18–19): there is no objective ground truth, and "Misleading critiques of good outputs may be indistinguishable from good critiques of poor outputs". The approach assumes reasoning can be put into words. It assumes labelers' preferences can be reconciled. Evaluation is not always easier than generation.
- The task is easy for humans: "Humans take up to around ten minutes to do the task, so we do not observe much speed-up". The authors say this "might not be reproducible on harder tasks".
- Models are "under-optimized": SFT only, no RL. The setup is hard to replicate.
- Critique gains are concentrated in minor and coverage flaws. Fig. 2 shows the increase in accuracy flaws is only "modest".
- The scaling evidence is weak in places. On synthetic tasks "the story is less clear", and "we have no strong reason to believe positive critique scaling to be a fundamental trend".
- Model sizes are not given in parameters. Scale is reported as fine-tuning loss, and the models are "not directly comparable".
- Dated: these are 2022 GPT-3-era fine-tuned models, and the InstructGPT baselines are now old. It does not test separate critic and generator agents, prompted (untrained) critics, or tool-using critics.

BUILDS ON
Iterated amplification [CSA18] Christiano, Shlegeris, Amodei 2018. Debate [ICA18] Irving, Christiano, Amodei 2018. Recursive reward modeling [LKE+18] Leike et al. 2018. Scalable oversight [AOS+16] Amodei et al. 2016. RLHP [CLB+17] Christiano et al. 2017. Best-of-N against a reward model [SOW+20] Stiennon et al. 2020. InstructGPT baselines [OWJ+22] Ouyang et al. 2022. Topic-based summarisation [Dan05] Dang 2005 and [ZYY+21] Zhong et al. 2021. Natural-language feedback [SCC+22] Scheurer et al. 2022. Chain of thought [WWS+22b] Wei et al. 2022. Process over outcomes [SB22] Stuhlmüller & Byun 2022. Eliciting latent knowledge [CCX21] Christiano, Cotra, Xu 2021. Interactive proofs [GMR89], [Sha92], [BFL91]. Alex Gray is credited with coining the name "generator-discriminator gap".

CODE
Prompt format for the critique task (App. A.5, p.27). Critiqueability and critique go in one sequence, so the token after the question doubles as a gate.
```
{passage}
Question: {question}
Answer: {answer}
Are there any critiques for the above answer? If so, write one
{binary critiqueability}
{critique}
```
Score definition (p.5): critiqueability and helpfulness scores are "Pr[Yes]/(Pr[Yes]+Pr[No])", read from the logits.

Task interfaces (Table 1, p.3). These map well to graph nodes:
- Base: Q → A
- Critiqueability: Q, A → {Yes, No}
- Critique: Q, A → C
- Helpfulness: Q, A, C → {Yes, No}
- Conditional refinement: Q, A, C → A
- Direct refinement: Q, A → A

FIGURES
- Table 1, p.3: the six task interfaces. It shows a generator/critic/judge/refiner graph at a glance.
- Fig. 1, p.2: critiques found per condition, with and without assistance. It is the headline result in one chart.
- Fig. 4, p.10: self-critique helpfulness rising with scale while outputs get harder to critique. It shows two competing trends together.
- Fig. 6 and 7, p.13: conditional vs direct refinement vs best-of-8 by scale. It shows "only at scale" and the compute caveat quickly.
- Fig. 8, p.14: GDC gaps on summarisation. It is the visual for "models know more than they say".
- Fig. 14, p.34: naive debate (best-of-N critique helpfulness) plateaus below the direct discriminator. It is a caution for critic-only judge nodes.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean. Some line-break hyphenation and ligatures (ﬁ, ﬂ) remain, and the fraction in the score formula and the expression "1 − 1/2N" are flattened in the text.
- Figures 1–16 are images only, so I could not quote any per-model numbers from the plots. The CD and GD gap claims therefore have no figures beside them.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
